## Goal
This vignette explains how you can use `slicer` to compute
Wasserstein distances between univariate empirical distributions
as well as sliced Wasserstein distances between multivariate empirical 
distributions.

## Wasserstein distances between univariate empirical distributions
Let's first load the `slicer` package and set a random seed.
```{r setup}
library(slicer)
set.seed(20261127)
```

Given two empirical distributions on $\mathbb{R}$,

$$P = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m \delta_{x_i}$$
and

$$Q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \delta_{y_j},$$

we want to compute the Wasserstein distance of order $p \in [1, \infty)$.
This is defined as

$$\mathbf{W}_p(P, Q) := \min_{\substack{X \sim P \\ Y \sim Q}} \left(\mathbb{E}|X - Y|^p\right)^{1/p}.$$

The distributions $P$ and $Q$ are represented as the vectors (or matrices)
$x = (x_1, \dots, x_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 1}$ and 
$y = (y_1, \dots, y_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}$, respectively.
For instance,

```{r}
P <- c(rnorm(20, 14, 3), rnorm(8, 1, 8))
Q <- rcauchy(14, location = 9, scale = 4)
```

The **north-west corner** algorithm is used to compute exact Wasserstein
distances of order $p$.
The function `nw_corner_distance()` runs it.

```{r}
nw_corner_distance(P, Q, p = 2)
nw_corner_distance(P, Q, p = 1)
```

This algorithm is essentially a sorting operation with some bells and whistles.
When working with large presorted vectors, you can set the parameter value for
`presorted` to `TRUE` for some speed-up.

Typically, we will have several empirical distributions $P_1, \dots, P_N$.
The function `compute_all_distances()` takes a list of empirical distributions
represented as vectors (or matrices).
If we don't specify anything to the contrary, it will assume that the input
distributions are all univariate.
By default, it outputs the pairwise $p$-Wasserstein distances _raised to the $p$-th_power_.
(The reason is that, in practice, we will often )
Also by default, $p = 2$ is used.

```{r}
P1 <- runif(14, -1, 1)
P2 <- rcauchy(39)
P3 <- rnorm(41)
P4 <- 2*(rbinom(47, 1, 0.4) - 1.5)
pw_dists <- compute_all_distances(list(P1, P2, P3, P4))
pw_dists
```

The actual $\mathbf{W}_2$ distances can now be obtain by taking the square root:

```{r}
sqrt(pw_dists)
```

Different orders ($p$) can be specified, too:

```{r}
compute_all_distances(list(P1, P2, P3, P4), p = 1)
```


## Wasserstein distances between projected multivariate distributions
While it is possible to define Wasserstein distances between
$d$-dimensinal distributions for $d \geq 2$, these distances are expensive
to compute. Moreover, they are not Hilbertian.
However, what we can do is define a number of vectors 
$\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and 
compute $p$-Wasserstein distances between the projections of the distributions
onto these vectors.

More precisely, let $P_1, \dots, P_N$ be $d$-dimensional empirical distributions
and let $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_L$ be projection vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
We now compute

$$\mathbf{W}_p({\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_i, {\theta_{\ell}}_{\#}^{\star} P_j)$$
for all $\ell = 1, \dots, L, 1 \leq i < j \leq N$,
where $v_{\#}^{\star}Q$ is the pushforward (image) measure of $Q$
under the map $x \mapsto v^{\top}x$.

Using `slicer`, we can compute these $L \cdot N(N-1)/2$ pairwise distances as follows.
We represent each $d$-dimensional empirical distribution 

$$P_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{k = 1}^{n_i} \delta_{x_{i, k}},$$
with $x_{i,k} \in \mathbb{R}^d$,
as a matrix,

$$M_i = 
\begin{pmatrix}
  x^{\top}_{i, 1} \\
  \vdots \\
  x^{\top}_{i, n_i}
\end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times d}.$$

We put these matrices $M_1, \dots, M_N$ in a list.

Then, we define a matrix

$$\Theta = \begin{pmatrix} \theta_1 & \cdots & \theta_L \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times L}$$
that contains the projection vectors.
If we're just interested in obtaining Wasserstein distances between
the corresponding marginal distributions, we set $\Theta = I_d$.

Then, we feed the list of $M$-matrices and $\Theta$ to `compute_all_distances()`.
